channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Post-Stroke Depression and Determinants in Ethiopia; A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the prevalence and determinants of post-stroke depression (PSD) in Ethiopia, a low-resource setting where PSD remains understudied. The review included eight studies to quantify prevalence and identify risk factors, addressing a gap in global mental health disparities.
FINDINGS: The pooled prevalence of PSD in Ethiopia was 40.9% (95% CI: 26.52–55.28, p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 91.1%). Female sex (OR 3.51, 95% CI: 1.87–6.58), illiteracy (OR 2.02, 95% CI: 1.29–3.17), and age over 40 years (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 1.09–2.32) were significantly associated with higher odds of PSD.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by high heterogeneity and a small number of included studies (n=8), which may affect the reliability of pooled estimates. The associations identified are plausible but should be interpreted cautiously due to potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., stroke severity, socioeconomic status). The lack of standardized screening tools across studies further limits comparability. While the prevalence is high, the clinical significance of these determinants needs validation in prospective cohorts.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians in Ethiopia and similar settings should screen for PSD, particularly in women, older patients, and those with low literacy. However, due to methodological limitations, these findings should prompt local quality improvement initiatives rather than definitive practice changes. Further research with standardized assessments is needed to confirm causality and inform targeted interventions.

item.title: Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review assessed the benefits and harms of medical cannabis for adults with insomnia, synthesizing evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to inform clinical practice and policy. The review included nine studies (n=537) comparing medical cannabis with placebo or active comparators, focusing on sleep quality, total sleep time, adverse events, and other sleep-related outcomes.
FINDINGS: Compared with placebo, medical cannabis showed little to no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality/satisfaction (SMD -0.49, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.08; 7 studies, 374 participants; very low-certainty evidence), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; 6 studies, 194 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or daytime functioning (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.16; 5 studies, 144 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Quality of life showed a trend toward improvement (SMD 0.84, 95% CI -0.61 to 2.29; 3 studies, 95 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were slightly more frequent with medical cannabis (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; 3 studies, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence), though the absolute risk difference was not reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very uncertain due to high risk of bias, serious inconsistency (I² up to 91%), and imprecision in effect estimates. The small sample sizes and heterogeneity in formulations (e.g., plant-based vs. synthetic cannabinoids) limit generalizability. While adverse events were more common with medical cannabis, the clinical significance is unclear due to low certainty. The review highlights the need for larger, well-designed RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up to clarify efficacy and safety.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support medical cannabis as an effective treatment for insomnia. Clinicians should exercise caution given the uncertain benefits and potential for adverse events. Further research is needed before considering medical cannabis for insomnia in routine practice.

item.title: Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Gender-Diverse Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020) investigated how autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and autistic traits are assessed in gender-diverse populations, addressing a gap in diagnostic practices for this group.
FINDINGS: Of 28 included studies, only 6 (33%) used robust diagnostic criteria (e.g., DSM-5/ADOS), identifying 100 confirmed ASD cases among 1,855 participants (5.4%). The pooled prevalence of robust ASD diagnosis was 12% (95% CI: 7%-19%), while broader autism phenotype prevalence was 24% (95% CI: 17%-33%). Most studies relied on self-report or screening tools rather than standardized assessments.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests elevated ASD prevalence in gender-diverse groups, but methodological variability (e.g., reliance on non-diagnostic tools) and high risk of bias (per Joanna Briggs Institute tools) limit confidence. The pooled estimates may overstate true prevalence due to heterogeneity and lack of standardized diagnostic procedures. Training in ASD and gender diversity is needed to improve diagnostic accuracy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice often lacks rigorous ASD assessment in gender-diverse patients. Clinicians should prioritize standardized diagnostic tools (e.g., ADOS-2, DSM-5 criteria) and be cautious interpreting self-report or screening results until more robust evidence emerges.

item.title: Education and training interventions for healthcare workers to prevent sexual harassment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review evaluated whether education or training interventions for healthcare workers reduce sexual harassment or improve knowledge/skills in managing it. It included only two small RCTs (170 nurses) comparing one type of harassment training against another, with no studies versus no intervention.
FINDINGS: Moderate-certainty evidence showed a small increase in “sexual harassment prevention” knowledge (MD 4.74 points on an unspecified scale, 95 % CI 1.21–8.28; 2 RCTs, 168 participants). Low-certainty evidence suggested possible small gains in “prevention strategy” (MD 11.70, 95 % CI 2.56–20.85) but not in “coping behaviour” (MD 6.36, 95 % CI –6.84 to 19.56). No study measured harassment incidence, mental health outcomes, sick leave, turnover, or organisational climate.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited (two small Taiwanese nurse trials) and provides no direct evidence that training reduces harassment or improves mental health. Effect sizes are small and imprecise, and the GRADE rating is moderate to low. Risk of bias was judged low, but imprecision and indirectness (only nurses, only versus another training) limit external validity. Adverse effects and long-term outcomes were not assessed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify widespread implementation of sexual-harassment training as a preventive strategy in routine psychiatric care. Any adoption should be cautious, time-limited, and accompanied by rigorous outcome evaluation.

item.title: [Clinical evidence of acupuncture and moxibustion for depressive disorder: controversy, reflection and prospect].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical evidence for acupuncture and moxibustion in treating depressive disorder, focusing on guidelines, systematic reviews, and trials to assess integration into mainstream psychiatric care. It highlights deficiencies and proposes directions for future research.
FINDINGS: The review identifies inconsistent recommendations across guidelines, methodological limitations in trials (e.g., small sample sizes, heterogeneity in techniques), and gaps in efficacy evaluation. Key issues include lack of standardized protocols, unclear mechanisms, and poor integration of mechanistic research with clinical practice.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to design flaws, heterogeneity, and limited high-quality trials. While the review suggests potential benefits, current data are insufficient to support routine use in psychiatric care. Strengths include a comprehensive critique of existing research; weaknesses stem from the narrative nature of the review and absence of quantitative synthesis.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Acupuncture/moxibustion for depression remains investigational. Clinicians should await robust RCTs before considering integration, and prioritize evidence-based treatments in routine care. Further research should address methodological rigor and standardization.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across the suicide prevention continuum, including risk detection, clinician training, and patient-facing psychotherapeutic support. It synthesizes early evidence on AI’s promise and risks in psychiatry, focusing on suicidal ideation (SI) detection and clinical integration.
FINDINGS: The review highlights studies suggesting AI models may detect SI more sensitively than clinicians by analyzing linguistic patterns, with reported improvements in clinician confidence and accuracy when AI is used adjunctively in risk assessments. AI-based virtual patients are cited as enhancing training outcomes, while CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable support. However, most patient-facing AI tools remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated, raising concerns about safety and efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without systematic methods or quantitative synthesis, this paper provides a conceptual overview rather than definitive evidence. The claims rely on selected studies without clear effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values, limiting the strength of conclusions. While the potential of AI is intriguing, the lack of rigorous validation and regulatory oversight underscores a critical gap between promise and clinical reality. The review appropriately flags ethical and safety risks but does not quantify harms or benefits.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI tools for suicide prevention should not replace standard clinical practice due to unproven efficacy and regulatory gaps. Clinicians should be aware of patient use of unvalidated AI tools and advocate for evidence-based integration. Further high-quality research—particularly randomized trials and regulatory frameworks—is urgently needed before AI can be recommended in routine care.

item.title: On the research on youth mental health: A scientometric analysis across mental disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scientometric analysis mapped global research trends on youth mental health across disorders from 1985 to 2025, aiming to identify evolving priorities and gaps in the evidence base for adolescents and young adults.
FINDINGS: The study included 65,684 publications, revealing shifting foci: prevalence/outcomes in the 1980s; assessment tools and pharmacotherapy in the 1990s–2000s; early intervention for psychosis, ADHD, eating disorders, and suicide in the 2010s; and global burden, access to care, and COVID-19 in the 2020s. Novel 2023–2025 trends included substance use, lifestyle psychiatry, and non-suicidal self-injury. Most research originated from Western countries, with underrepresentation of lived experience involvement, open science, implementation research, and social determinants.
INTERPRETATION: As a scientometric analysis, this study provides a high-level overview of research trajectories rather than causal evidence. Strengths include its comprehensive scope and temporal mapping, but limitations include reliance on bibliometric data (not quality assessment) and geographic skew toward Western settings. The findings highlight evolving priorities but do not quantify clinical effectiveness or guide specific interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study underscores the need for broader, more inclusive research agendas in youth mental health, particularly addressing understudied areas like lived experience leadership and social determinants, but does not directly inform bedside practice.

item.title: Reducing Caregiver Burden in First-Episode Psychosis: Effects of a Psychoeducational Pathway Led by an Advanced Practice Nurse-A Multicentre Stepped-Wedge Randomized Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Family caregivers of people with first-episode psychosis (FEP) often experience high psychological distress and lack structured support. This multicentre stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial (RCT) in France evaluates whether a psychoeducational pathway led by advanced practice nurses (APNs) reduces caregiver burden over 6 months.
FINDINGS: The trial included six FEP centres and compared the APN-led psychoeducational pathway (initial consultation, single-family BREF programme, and multifamily PEPs Aidant programme) against usual care. The primary outcome was change in caregiver burden (measured by the Zarit Burden Interview) from baseline to 6 months. Secondary outcomes included caregiver mood (HADS), self-efficacy, quality of life, and patient engagement and recovery perception. The trial followed SPIRIT guidelines and was registered (NCT07041463). Quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The stepped-wedge RCT design is appropriate for evaluating complex interventions in real-world settings, but the abstract lacks key quantitative results (effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, sample size, dropout). Without these, the magnitude and clinical significance of any observed reduction in caregiver burden remain unclear. The qualitative component will provide insight into implementation processes but does not address efficacy. The study’s external validity may be limited to French FEP services with APN capacity, and generalisability to other healthcare systems is uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This trial could inform the development of structured caregiver support pathways in FEP services, particularly if APNs are available. However, without published results, no changes to current practice can be recommended yet. Clinicians should await the full publication for effect sizes and feasibility data before considering adoption.

item.title: The effect of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope among individuals with schizophrenia: A single-blind randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-blind RCT (n=44) in a Turkish Community Mental Health Center tested whether adding psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing to routine care improves schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope compared with routine care alone in adults with schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: At baseline, groups were balanced (p > .05). Post-intervention, the intervention group showed large gains in knowledge (F = 176.060, p < .001, η² = 0.898) and hope (F = 99.782, p < .001, η² = 0.833), which persisted at one-month follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: The very large effect sizes and statistical significance suggest a robust short-term impact, but the single-centre design, small sample, and lack of assessor blinding raise risks of performance and detection bias. The follow-up is only one month, so durability beyond this horizon is unknown. Funding sources were not reported, so industry or academic bias cannot be excluded.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing may modestly boost insight and hope, but current evidence is preliminary; centres should pilot the programme while monitoring longer-term outcomes and adherence before widespread adoption.

item.title: The effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence in individuals with bipolar disorder: A randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a Swedish Community Mental Health Center (CMHC) tested whether structured tele-nursing counseling (weekly telephone calls plus supportive text messages for 8 weeks) improves functioning and medication adherence in 70 adults with bipolar disorder compared with usual care.
FINDINGS: After 8 weeks, the intervention group showed a mean improvement in FAST score of 6.8 points better than controls (95 % CI –9.8 to –3.7; p < 0.001) and a 2.11-point greater increase in MMAS adherence (95 % CI –2.4 to –1.8; p < 0.001), both adjusted for baseline values.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is small (n = 70) and of short duration (8 weeks), with no long-term follow-up or blinding of assessors. The effect sizes (≈7 FAST points; ≈2 MMAS points) are statistically significant but of uncertain clinical magnitude; minimal clinically important differences for FAST and MMAS are not established in this population. The study was retrospectively registered, raising minor concerns about outcome-reporting bias. Overall, the evidence is suggestive but preliminary.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Tele-nursing counseling may modestly improve short-term functioning and adherence in bipolar disorder, but larger, longer, and independently registered trials are needed before recommending routine adoption.

item.title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study explores whether a gene-targeted mRNA therapy could address a mechanistic gap in schizophrenia treatment, focusing on rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in the GRIA3 gene encoding the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. The study integrates population-based genetic screening, family-based validation, and animal modeling to justify a potential therapeutic approach.
FINDINGS: In a U.S. healthcare system cohort of 30,813 schizophrenia patients, two female relatives carried a rare PTV in GRIA3. Family analysis suggested an X-linked inheritance pattern linking the PTV to severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in patient-derived neurons restored GRIA3 expression. An mRNA drug targeting GRIA3 was developed and tested in mice, showing good tolerability, broad brain expression of GluA3, and reversal of MK-801–induced behavioral abnormalities (a pharmacological psychosis model).
INTERPRETATION: This is a proof-of-concept study combining genetic discovery, cellular validation, and animal efficacy data. While the findings are promising—especially the functional rescue of neuronal deficits and behavioral abnormalities—they are preliminary and far removed from clinical application. The study is limited by its reliance on a single family, lack of human data, and use of a non-disease–specific animal model. The translational path to human trials will require addressing safety, delivery, and efficacy in more clinically relevant models.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this research does not change clinical practice but signals a potential future gene-targeted therapeutic avenue for a subset of patients with rare GRIA3 variants. Clinicians should be aware of emerging precision medicine approaches in psychiatry but should not expect immediate impact on treatment decisions.

item.title: Exploring the feasibility, safety and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted temporal interference stimulation for major depressive disorder: a pilot study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a novel noninvasive neuromodulation technique. However, whether it can be applied in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. This pilot study investigated the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted TIS in patients with MDD. METHODS: In this single-center, single-arm pilot study, 32 MDD patients received a 5-day amygdala-targeted TIS.

item.title: Differential changes in frontolimbic functional connectivity following 12-week psychostimulant monotherapy in ADHD youth with and without familial risk for bipolar I disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Although attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), psychostimulant medications, and BD family history are risk factors for developing bipolar I disorder (BD), their contribution to the aberrant ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) and amygdala (AMY) functional connectivity (FC) implicated in the pathophysiology of BD remain unclear.

item.title: The relationship between physical activity and mental health in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A scoping review.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at risk of developing secondary mental health problems. Physical activity (PA) has recently gained attention as a non-pharmacological intervention. However, studies that comprehensively organize its effects on different aspects of mental health remain limited. This study aimed to systematically organize existing evidence on the effects of PA on the mental health of children with ADHD. METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

item.title: Pain-contingent opioid use and addiction risk in cancer pain: a reappraisal of around-the-clock dosing.
item.description: Around-the-clock (ATC) opioid dosing has anchored cancer pain management since an era of advanced disease, continuous pain, and short survival, when undertreatment was the dominant clinical failure. Contemporary oncology increasingly involves prolonged survival and chronic treatment-related pain, and advances in behavioral pharmacology and addiction neuroscience challenge the assumption that dosing schedules are behaviorally neutral.

item.title: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome Following Three Randomized Controlled Trials of Choline in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD).
item.description: BACKGROUND: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) represents a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes from prenatal alcohol exposure for which there are few interventions. Preclinical studies have identified choline as a potential treatment for cognitive deficits in FASD. We previously conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children under age 6 and reported on memory benefits following all three trials. Two RCTs compared a fixed 500 mg daily dose to placebo, and the third RCT tested a weight-adjusted choline dose.

item.title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression.

item.title: Comparing family history indicators and polygenic scores in depressive disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Genetic liability of depressive disorder can be captured by psychopathology in relatives (family history). Various methods summarize family history in a single score, differing in included information as well as the underlying model. We systematically compared the performance of family history indicators, including promising new indicators based on the liability threshold model, in predicting depressive disorder.

item.title: Assessing the effect of subthalamic stimulation on metaperception in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description: Most human studies on perceptual decision-making are correlational, and few addressed the causal role of the neural markers they identify. Here, we took the opportunity offered by deep brain stimulation to study the causal role of subthalamo-cortical networks on perceptual decision-making and perceptual monitoring. We asked participants with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) treated with subthalamic stimulation to detect visual stimuli and provide confidence reports while we recorded scalp electroencephalography.

item.title: Universal suicide risk assessment for veterans and soldiers in all healthcare settings: A nursing imperative.
item.description: PURPOSE: Suicide remains a major public health concern among U.S. veterans and active-duty military personnel. This narrative review examines evidence supporting routine suicide risk screening and considers its implementation as a clinically appropriate, trauma-informed process rather than an inflexible requirement at every encounter. METHODS: A structured narrative review used targeted searches of PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus, supplemented by federal surveillance reports, clinical guidance, and policy documents.

item.title: Drug Use Patterns and Characteristics by Drug Type Among Drug Abusers: Findings From the Survey of Drug Abusers in Korea 2021.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Although substance use disorders are increasingly recognized in the Republic of Korea (South Korea), empirical data on the prevalence and characteristics of drug use among treatment-seeking populations remain limited. This study examined the rate and temporal patterns of major psychoactive substance use-specifically sedatives/hypnotics/tranquilizers (sedatives), amphetamines, and marijuana/cannabis (cannabis)-across three timeframes and explored the associated sociodemographic and clinical factors.

item.title: Alcohol-involved suicide mortality prevalence estimates and identification of co-occurring substance use from the National Violent Death Reporting System, 2022-2023.
item.description: Using National Violent Death Reporting System data (2022-2023), 14 909 suicide decedents (34%) tested positive for alcohol. The most common substances co-occurring with alcohol were marijuana, antidepressants, opioids, and benzodiazepines; polysubstance use was high, with 52% testing positive for alcohol and ≥1 other substance. Findings suggest an overall alcohol-involved suicide mortality rate of 24%, appearing higher than prior estimates.

item.title: Reductions in PTSD symptom clusters among perinatal and postnatal survivors of intimate partner violence participating in the Heartbeats program.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a leading cause of injury among women, especially during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Experiencing IPV increases the risk of mental health disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD during the perinatal period is associated with poorer maternal mental health and adverse early child outcomes. Heartbeats (HB) is a hospital-based, community-linked violence intervention program designed to reduce morbidity and mortality among perinatal and postnatal survivors of IPV.

item.title: Acute Ultra Low Dose THC Attenuates Anxiety-Like Behavior in a Mouse Model for Major-Depressive Disorder.
item.description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent psychiatric disorder, and is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Current treatments for MDD entail many side effects, and include a lag until the onset of therapeutic effects. The current hypotheses as for the etiology of MDD revolve around the monoamine hypothesis and the plasticity and neurodegeneration hypothesis. According to the latter, employing a neuroprotective treatment may help ameliorate depressive symptoms. Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the primary psychoactive component of the cannabis sativa plant.

item.title: A pilot postpartum depression intervention in rural Indiana: Recruitment barriers, retention, and implementation lessons.
item.description: Rural postpartum women face substantial barriers to evidence-based treatment for postpartum depression (PPD). The purpose of this study was to evaluate recruitment, retention, intervention delivery, and acceptability of a four-session, group-based pilot intervention adapted for rural Indiana. An open pilot feasibility study was conducted at two rural health systems. Feasibility outcomes were compared with prespecified recruitment and retention thresholds; acceptability and participant symptom scores were summarized descriptively.

item.title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder as a Risk Factor for Suicidality in Patients With Borderline Personality Disorder.
item.description: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are each associated with impulsivity, emotion dysregulation, and an increased prevalence of suicide attempts. It is unclear whether comorbid ADHD heightens suicide risk in individuals with BPD. This study examined suicide attempts among psychiatric outpatients diagnosed with either comorbid BPD and ADHD (n = 54) or BPD without ADHD (n = 330). Patients were assessed with several semistructured interviews.

item.title: Geographical disparities in intentional self-harm hospitalization risks in Florida: a retrospective ecological study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Over the last decade, intentional self-harm hospitalization risks have increased in the United States (US). Although there is evidence of geographic disparities in intentional self-harm hospitalization risks, with some areas having significantly higher risks, little is known about these disparities in Florida. Identifying these disparities is useful for guiding prevention programs and tailoring efforts to mitigate the problem. Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate geographic disparities of intentional self-harm hospitalization risks in Florida.

item.title: A psychiatric nurse-led awareness and peer support intervention for suicide prevention among university students.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate a suicide prevention program combining awareness training and peer support among university students. METHODS: A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design with an embedded qualitative component was conducted with 63 university students. The intervention was structured within a psychiatric nursing framework informed by Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory.

item.title: Mapping the self-compassion-suicidal ideation link: A serial multiple mediation path analysis involving basic psychological needs and ultra-processed food intake.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Recent lifestyle psychiatry research has highlighted the harmful effects of ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption on mental health. Although UPF intake has been linked to depression and anxiety, its association with suicidal ideation remains underexplored. The psychological mechanisms underlying this relationship, particularly the roles of self-compassion and basic psychological needs, are also unclear. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey included 400 Japanese adults aged 20-59, stratified by national age distribution.

item.title: Basic Psychological Needs and Sustained Participation in Men's Sheds: Implications for Well-Being and Suicide Prevention.
item.description: Older men who endorse traditional masculine values such as stoicism and independence may be less likely to seek help when distressed, increasing vulnerability to social isolation and suicide. Men's Sheds, operating in 12 countries with around 3,000 sheds, offer practical activities, shared purpose, and informal social connection in settings that align with familiar masculine norms while providing support. Despite these benefits, many sheds struggle to maintain member engagement, and little is known about why some men remain involved over the long term while others disengage.

item.title: Plasma chromogranin a levels and their role in the etiology of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Anxiety disorder is a common psychiatric condition in pediatric populations that may become chronic and impair functioning if left untreated. Chromogranin A (CgA) is a polypeptide co-secreted with catecholamines in response to stress and anxiety. The association between CgA and anxiety disorder has been investigated in adult populations; however, data in children and adolescents remain limited.

item.title: The serial mediation of embodied self-representation and psychological flexibility in the relationship between boredom proneness and depression among individuals with schizophrenia.
item.description: A significant research gap persists in delineating the cardinal difficulties associated with negative symptoms throughout the trajectory of psychosis, highlighting the need for increased clinical vigilance. To investigate the associations between embodied self-representation, psychological flexibility, boredom proneness, and depression in individuals with schizophrenia (IwS), and to examine whether embodied self-representation and psychological flexibility serially mediate this relationship, a cross-sectional research design was used.

item.title: A mixed-methods study of mental health and trauma among women in the sex work industry in Spain.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The sexual commerce industry significantly impacts the psychological health of prostituted women. This study examines mental health damages and complex trauma in 12 women exposed to this commerce. The goal of this work was to evaluate the mental health damage and trauma-related symptoms of these women at the beginning of an intervention. METHODS: A mixed methodology was used. Quantitatively, four measures were administered to assess subjective distress, the depression-anxiety-stress triad, post-traumatic stress disorder, and cumulative trauma in everyday life.

item.title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus.
item.description: Recursive splice sites are rare motifs postulated to facilitate splicing across massive introns and shape isoform diversity. The necessity of recursive splicing (RS) and its role in human disease are unsubstantiated. Here, we use CRISPR to model intronic deletions eliminating an RS site (RS1) in CADM2 and conferring risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and other neurobehavioral traits. Ablating RS1 in human induced neurons alters the gradient of RNA abundance across CADM2's first intron, decreases CADM2 expression, and impacts transcript usage.

item.title: Scalp Topography of Event-Related Potentials Reveals Differences in Audiovisual Speech Processing in Autistic and Non-Autistic Children.
item.description: PURPOSE: In our prior work, conventional event-related potential (ERP) responses to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech were found to explain variance in language abilities in autistic and non-autistic children but failed to differentiate autistic children from non-autistic children.

item.title: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
item.description: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being.

item.title: Long-Term Treatment Patterns in Norwegian ADHD-Medicine Users: A Cohort Register-Based Study With 5 Years of Follow-Up, 2012-2021.
item.description: PURPOSE: To improve interpretation of long-term ADHD medication treatment trajectories in Norway by examining sex- and age-specific persistence, distinguishing within-substance product switching from active-ingredient (ATC substance) switching, and describing the medication and prescriber context of the last observed dispensation before non-persistence. METHODS: This study used population-based data from the Norwegian Prescription Database (NorPD) to identify 33 706 incident users initiating ADHD medication in 2012-2016, defined using an individual-specific 5-year look-back.

item.title: Comparison of Natural Language Processing and Traditional Qualitative Analyses of Caregiver Feedback From a Community-Based Intervention for Children With Autism.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Satisfaction data is a commonly used construct to evaluate programs, products, and experiences. This data is collected through forced choice (scales, surveys) and/or open-ended measures. While open-ended questions have the greatest potential for more useful and candid feedback, analysis of this data can be time-consuming.

item.title: Exploring Transdiagnostic Mechanisms Linking Borderline Personality Disorder and Disordered Eating.
item.description: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occurs with eating disorders (EDs). Disordered eating may serve as a coping strategy to regulate emotions/manage rejection sensitivity, abandonment fears, shame, and self-disgust. Research examining disordered eating in BPD remains limited. This study explored ED pathology/related psychological constructs in adults diagnosed with BPD. Eighty participants completed questionnaires assessing BPD symptom severity, ED pathology, childhood trauma, cognitive distortions, shame, self-disgust, coping, personality traits, and emotion regulation.

item.title: What Is True for Others Does Not Apply to Me: Expectations About Social Causality and the Anticipation of Emotions in Borderline Personality Disorder.
item.description: Research suggests that individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD) display a maladaptive explanatory style, but it remains unclear whether this bias is specific to self-referential processing or reflects a broader negative tendency. We examined whether expectations about self-esteem-damaging and self-esteem-enhancing explanations, as well as associated emotions, are specific to self-referential processing in BPD, and how they relate to self-esteem and loneliness.

item.title: Migration Characteristics and Mechanism of Active Components From Jieyu Anshen Granule in Different Insomnia Mouse Models.
item.description: RATIONALE: Insomnia is a highly prevalent disorder with substantial health and socioeconomic impacts, for which traditional Chinese medicine is an important treatment option. Jieyu Anshen Granule (JYAS-G) shows excellent clinical efficacy in insomnia treatment, but its active components, in vivo migration characteristics and underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

item.title: Executive Summary of the Clinical Practice Guideline on Tinnitus Update.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is an evidence-based clinical practice guideline update on the evaluation and management of persistent, bothersome tinnitus in adults (≥18 years). It aims to provide clinicians with actionable recommendations to improve care and mitigate the impact of tinnitus on quality of life, excluding cases with identifiable non-SNHL causes, objective/pulsatile tinnitus, transient symptoms, or hallucinations.
FINDINGS: The guideline includes 15 Key Action Statements (KASs), with strong recommendations for distinguishing bothersome from nonbothersome tinnitus (KAS 2), assessing suicide risk (KAS 3), avoiding routine neuroradiologic imaging unless red flags are present (KAS 6), and recommending CBT for persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 11). It advises against routine use of antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, dietary supplements, or rTMS for primary tinnitus treatment (KAS 12–14A). Recommendations include performing targeted history/physical exams (KAS 1), audiological evaluation (KAS 5), patient education (KAS 7), hearing aid evaluation (KAS 8), cochlear implant referral when criteria are met (KAS 9), sound enrichment (KAS 10), bimodal neuromodulation (KAS 14B), and routine outcome assessment (KAS 15).
INTERPRETATION: This guideline is based on a structured evidence review and consensus process by a multidisciplinary Guideline Update Group. Strengths include clear scope, exclusion of non-generalizable cases, and prioritization of interventions with supportive evidence (e.g., CBT). Limitations include reliance on low-to-moderate quality evidence for many recommendations, heterogeneity in tinnitus etiologies, and lack of direct comparative data for newer interventions (e.g., bimodal neuromodulation). The recommendations against pharmacologic and device-based therapies reflect insufficient high-quality evidence rather than proven inefficacy. External validity is limited to adults with persistent, bothersome tinnitus, primarily related to SNHL.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize CBT, audiological assessment, and patient education for persistent, bothersome tinnitus. Routine imaging and pharmacologic treatments are not recommended unless specific indications arise. Newer options like sound enrichment and bimodal neuromodulation may be considered on an individualized basis, but evidence remains preliminary.

item.title: Network Meta-Analysis: Treatments for Acute Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) has high short-term mortality, and multiple treatments have been tested in randomised trials. This systematic review and network meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy of treatments for AH based on 90-day survival, synthesising data from randomised studies to guide future research.
FINDINGS: Thirty-five randomised studies (n=5045) examined 24 treatments. Only granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (GCSF) showed a statistically significant benefit on 90-day mortality compared to placebo (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.28–0.84; p=0.009). In subgroup analyses restricted to low-risk-of-bias studies, no treatment effect remained significant.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and dominated by small trials, limiting precision and reliability. The apparent benefit of GCSF is not robust when restricted to higher-quality studies, suggesting potential publication bias or confounding. Effect sizes are large but confidence intervals wide, and no treatment can be recommended based on current evidence. Further adequately powered, high-quality randomised trials are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No treatment can currently be recommended for routine use in AH based on 90-day survival. Clinicians should await results of larger, well-designed trials before considering agents like GCSF outside research settings.

item.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus Update.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a clinical practice guideline update on the management of persistent, bothersome tinnitus in adults (18+ years) from the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Foundation. It aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for evaluation and treatment to improve symptoms and quality of life.
FINDINGS: The guideline includes 15 Key Action Statements (KASs): 3 strong recommendations (e.g., assess suicide risk in bothersome tinnitus; avoid routine neuroradiologic imaging unless red flags are present), 9 recommendations (e.g., perform targeted history/physical exam; obtain audiological evaluation; educate patients; recommend CBT), 2 recommendations against (e.g., not routinely using antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, dietary supplements), and 3 options (e.g., may inquire about somatosensory features; may recommend sound enrichment; may offer bimodal neuromodulation). No numerical effect sizes or p-values are reported, as this is a guideline.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of evidence lies in the multidisciplinary guideline development process and broad stakeholder involvement, enhancing face validity. However, as a guideline, it synthesizes existing evidence rather than generating new data; the recommendations are graded based on the quality of underlying studies, which vary in rigor. The absence of quantitative outcomes limits assessment of clinical significance. The recommendations against pharmacologic treatments and rTMS reflect limited high-quality evidence supporting their efficacy for tinnitus per se. External validity is high for otolaryngology and audiology settings but may be less applicable to psychiatric care unless tinnitus is comorbid with mental health conditions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For psychiatrists, the key takeaway is the strong recommendation to assess suicide risk in patients with bothersome tinnitus and to consider referral for CBT, which is supported by this guideline. Routine use of antidepressants or other medications solely for tinnitus is discouraged unless there is a comorbid psychiatric indication. Sound-based therapies and CBT remain first-line non-pharmacologic options.

item.title: Development and non-randomized pilot trial of Families FORWARD: a new program for families of autistic youth transitioning to adulthood.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: Autistic youth and their families describe transitioning to adulthood as overwhelming. Yet, there are few evidence-based, family focused transition programs broad enough to serve youths' wide range of autism-related and background characteristics. We report on the community-engaged development of Families FORWARD (Focusing On Relationships, Well-being, And Responsibility aheaD), a new family based, individualized transition planning program (Phase 1) and non-randomized pilot trial findings regarding acceptability, feasibility, and clinical promise (Phase 2).

item.title: Sociodemographic, Criminological and Clinical Determinants in Suicide After Release From Prison: A 23-Year National Cohort Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Suicide risk is elevated after prison release, but population-level evidence on temporal risk patterns and associated factors remains limited. We aimed to describe characteristics of individuals who die by suicide after release from Norwegian prisons, compare their suicide mortality with the general population, and examine risk factors over time.

item.title: Perceptions of a Community-Based Perinatal Mental Health Intervention.
item.description: Mental health concerns are the leading complication of childbearing and have long-lasting impacts on maternal outcomes and infants' social, emotional and cognitive development. The Growing Hope Kit was founded on an evidence-based intervention (hope box) and developed using the Social-Ecological Model, positive psychology framework and Sources of Strength. The Kit included information and activities to enhance distress tolerance, coping strategies based on cognitive behavioral and dialectical behavioral therapies, mental wellness and parenting skills.

item.title: Drug Repurposing for Treating NCOR-Related Intellectual Disability.
item.description: Nuclear receptor corepressors (NCOR1/2) mediate the transcriptional activity of methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2), and genetic variants in NCOR1/2 or MECP2 associate with autism or intellectual disability. However, it is unknown whether heterozygous NCOR mutations impair cognitive functions and how NCOR-related intellectual disability can be treated. Here, we constructed a knock-in (KI) mouse line carrying a heterozygous NCOR1 mutation (NCOR1 c.2182+2T>G) found in a pediatric patient.

item.title: ADHD symptoms and learning difficulties: co-occurrence and directionality from Grades 1 to 9.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at increased risk of learning difficulties. This association may reflect shared risk factors, ADHD symptoms hindering learning, or learning difficulties increasing ADHD symptoms. We aimed to map rates of co-occurrence among ADHD, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and reading comprehension difficulties and to investigate directional influences between ADHD symptoms and reading fluency, arithmetic, and reading comprehension.

item.title: Triangulation of dispensing and wastewater data for surveillance during lisdexamfetamine shortages: A descriptive time series analysis.
item.description: AIMS: Lisdexamfetamine, a long-acting stimulant for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), has experienced widespread shortages in Australia since late 2023, raising concerns about treatment continuity and shifts in stimulant use patterns. This study assessed the impact of shortages in South Australia (SA) and Western Australia (WA) by triangulating prescription dispensing and wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE).
